title: Understand how to use keys, Postgres types and keywords
summary: Recaps tables, columns and rows, then shows how a table is declared in Postgres: PRIMARY KEY, SERIAL auto-increment, and the common column types VARCHAR, CHAR, TEXT, INT and BOOLEAN, using a friends table as the running example.

concepts.heading: Tables, columns and rows
points: A column is a vertical field (name, age, ...) that describes one characteristic of the data. A row is a horizontal record, one entry such as one friend.
A database is a set of tables linked by relationships and rules for how they behave.
Compared with spreadsheets, databases stay fast with huge record counts (millions of rows), whereas a spreadsheet gets sluggish after a few thousand.

concepts.heading: CREATE TABLE in Postgres
points: Syntax: CREATE TABLE table_name ( field_name type constraints, ... ); with the whole definition ending in a semicolon.
Each field is written as its name, then its data type, then optional keywords. Fields are separated by commas inside the parentheses.
Postgres has a larger set of types than the basic SQL ones seen earlier.

concepts.heading: PRIMARY KEY and SERIAL
points: PRIMARY KEY marks the column whose values must be unique and which uniquely identifies each record. Two friends can share a name, so a name is not a safe way to pick out one row; an id is.
SERIAL is a Postgres type for auto-incrementing integers: when inserting a new row you leave id out and Postgres gives it the next number (previous + 1).
id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY is therefore the standard first column of a table.
BIGSERIAL is the same idea with a much larger range, for tables that could reach billions of rows.

concepts.heading: Character types: VARCHAR, CHAR, TEXT
points: VARCHAR(50) means variable-length text with a maximum of 50 characters. A 4-letter value only uses the space it needs.
CHAR(50) is fixed-length: it reserves room for 50 characters whatever the actual data length, so it is less efficient for varying text.
TEXT has no declared maximum and also uses only the space needed.

Older advice favoured VARCHAR with a limit for efficiency. Modern tests on very large databases show TEXT is only marginally slower or larger, and it avoids failures when a value turns out longer than expected.
Rule of thumb: use VARCHAR(n) when you truly know the maximum size; use TEXT when you want flexibility. Both are acceptable.

concepts.heading: Numbers and booleans
points: BOOLEAN stores true or false, suited to yes/no fields such as is_cool.
The Postgres documentation lists many more types (dates, character varying and others) and is worth skimming.

(Extra) Inserting without an id; SERIAL fills it in
code_examples.code: INSERT INTO friends (name, age, is_cool) VALUES ('Jack', 20, true);

pitfalls: Using a non-unique field such as name to identify a row; use the primary key.
Declaring CHAR(n) when values vary in length (wasted space, and fixed-width padding).
Setting VARCHAR limits too small and later hitting values that do not fit.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'Postgres column types and keys': blurb on columns/rows, PRIMARY KEY, SERIAL, VARCHAR vs TEXT.

Tasks: (1) write CREATE TABLE for a books table with id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, (2) choose the right type for each of 6 sample fields, (3) spot why a duplicate id would fail, (4) rewrite a CHAR(50) column as VARCHAR or TEXT and justify it.
Starter code: a half-finished CREATE TABLE friends with blank types.

Interactive demo: a table builder where you add columns and types and watch a sample row grid and the generated SQL update, with a toggle that shows the storage size difference between CHAR(50) and VARCHAR(50).
